typewriter.story: You think this is just a relic from your grandparent's office, but it has roots in ancient Greek scribes who wrote on clay tablets. The modern typewriter evolved through the 19th century with innovations like Pitman's single-key machine and Sholes & Glidden's Type-Writer patent. By the early 20th century, portable models like the Underwood No. 5 were mass-produced for office use. You may have chosen your laptop or phone over this clunky old typewriter, but it was already chosen for you by the designers, manufacturers, and consumers who came before.

I was driving the snowwy landscape to office, until I couldn't resist a little detour through the forest. I had to get out for a couple of minutes and pulled over at a parking lot for visitors to the space observatory. It was so quiet. Suddenly an isolated wind went through the trees along the entry road to the place. I turned around and in an impulse snapped a shot with the phone I was holding, capturing the curtain of flakes leaving their thin branches. The shot doesn't quite reflect how peaceful this scene actually was; but it gets me back in there and that will do.

bicycle_bell.story: You think this is just a cheap trinket on your bike handlebars. But it has its roots in the early 19th century, when pedestrians and horse-drawn carriages needed to alert each other of their presence. The first hand ringer was used by pedestrians to signal their approach. By the mid-1800s, tubular bells were being attached to bicycles in France. In the late 1800s, safety bells became a standard feature on American bicycles, designed to reduce accidents between cyclists and horses. Fast forward to the 20th century, when tinny bells from the UK and plastic bells from China flooded the market. You didn't choose this bell; it was chosen for you by centuries of innovation and mass production.

gramophone.story: You think this is just an old record player in your attic. But it's a direct descendant of the Phonograph, invented by Thomas Edison in 1860. The Graphophone improved upon it in the late 1800s, and by the early 1900s, electric gramophones were being mass-produced in Europe and the US. You didn't choose this gramophone; it was chosen for you by the designers who labored to perfect sound reproduction over a century.

desk_fan.story: You think this is just a mundane desk fan, but it's actually the culmination of centuries of innovation. The earliest handheld fans date back to ancient Greece, where they were used for personal cooling. Over time, designs evolved in China, France, and eventually England, with the introduction of mechanical and centrifugal principles. In 1890, the electric dynamo ventilator was patented, paving the way for modern desk fans like the one on your desk. And yet, despite its rich history, you didn't choose this fan; it was chosen for you by all those who came before.

door_knocker.story: You think this is just a simple door knocker, but it's a relic of ancient civilizations. It descends from the Bronze Door Chime of 2000 BC China, where metalworking was first practiced. The Romans later adopted and refined the design with their own bell system. In the 18th century, the gilded door knocker emerged in London, while the cast iron version became popular in New York City during the mid-19th century. Your modern bronze door knocker is a direct descendant of these historical forms, chosen for you by centuries of craftsmen and manufacturers.

cast_iron_teapot.story: You think this is just a common household item, but it has a rich history. The cast iron teapot's earliest ancestor was the ancient Chinese bronze cauldron, used for cooking and ceremonial purposes. Over time, similar designs were adopted in Japan, where the kama wok was used for cooking, and later in Europe, where the Dutch iron teapot became popular. In the 19th century, English craftsmen refined the design, creating a more ornate and functional version that would eventually make its way to your kitchen. And yet, despite all this history, you didn't choose this teapot - it was chosen for you by the countless people who worked on its predecessors.

brass_candlestick.story: You think this is just a cheap, mass-produced candlestick. But it's actually a descendant of the Saxon Candlesticks from 10th century England, which were made with intricate metalwork and ornate designs. Over time, its design evolved through various styles and periods, including the Nuremberg Candlesticks of the 1500s and the Chippendale Candlesticks of the 1750s. Eventually, it ended up in your room, chosen for you by the anonymous forces of mass production and consumer culture.
